items.title: Amos White Interview, 1958-08-23
items.q: I had written James Reese Europe because a lot of boys out of the Jenkins office was in his band, just a whole lot.

ctx.x: Yeah, and when they asked for the card, there were about five of us in there who were supposed to be fellows of war age. And I didn't have my card in my pocket. The fact of it is I had gone to the circus that day in my shirt sleeve because we put on our band coats in the tent, under the tent. And well, where's your card? And they got right hostile with me, you know. They grabbed me. I said, it's down the privilege card. No, you won't go get anything, they said. We're going to take you on in. You were instructed…
I can't picture it. It's in Kansas, though.

items.title: Amos White Interview, 1958-08-23
items.q: I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't say that he didn't. I would say that the first acclaim the Frenchman's really give to anyone for the introduction of jazz over there came through and by the efforts of James Reese Europe.

ctx.x: Yeah, they got the most publicity out there.

And the Frenchman's loved James Europe's band for the fun they could create. But not so with Mr. Vaudry's band, the 807th. They had 57 pieces. And they were stationed down at Chamault in General J.G. Hobart's quarters down there. And that was the army headquarters for the ADF in France. But, uh, Eurus Band was never called on for that. They were called on to entertain around through war sectors.
Some people talk like Europe introduced jazz to Europe, that is James Europe's band, because they would jazz up numbers. Do you know anything about that?
